sections.text:
1 Die 11 maii anni ͵ςωληʹ (= 1330 p. C. n.) genituram Constantinopolis compo-
suerunt astrologi, vide cod. Taurin. 4, f. 51. Non de refectione moenium ab Andro-
nico agitur (ibid., cod. 5, f. 40; p. 15, n. 1); sed post mille annos urbem regiam quasi
novam vitam incepisse docuerunt mathematici, ni fallor, nam eam die 11 Maii
anni 330 conditam fuisse Byzantini credebant; cf. Preger, Das Gründungsdatum
von Konstantinopel (Hermes, XXXVI), 1901, p. 336 ss.
sections.en: 1 On the 11th of May of the year 6838 (= 1330 A.D.) astrologers composed the nativity of Constantinople, see cod. Taurin. 4, f. 51. It is not about the rebuilding of the walls by Andronicus (ibid., cod. 5, f. 40; p. 15, n. 1); but mathematicians taught that after a thousand years the royal city began a new life, if I am not mistaken, for the Byzantines believed it was founded on the 11th of May of the year 330; cf. Preger, Das Gründungsdatum von Konstantinopel (Hermes, XXXVI), 1901, p. 336 ss.

summary.headline: Astrological Chapters 241–252
summary.text: Astrological chapter list and commentary on perambulations of stars and places, including the nativity of Constantinople, annual zodiacal rulers, world nativity, seventh-house marriage questions, hermaphrodite desire, life, superiority, death, and thieves and stolen goods. Authorities and cross-references include Eleutherios Zebelenos, Demophilos, and several Venetian, Vindobonese, and Milanese codices.
